title: My thoughts on the defendant's innocence in 12 Angry Men

commenti.body: Tbh I don’t think there *exists* an answer. Same with films like Doubt for example, I think the film does a good enough job in focusing on ambiguity and constant switches in your thinking that I’m convinced there exists no answer. The directors and writers etc didn’t have a definitive answer in mind, the film purely is about the process.

Yeah. I think its largely the point of the movie that you don't know for sure lol. If you don't know for sure, you're obligated to vote Not Guilty. Its a film about the foundational ethics of American morality and justice.

Definitely morally ambiguous, the defendant, but the thing is, _he_ is not really the subject of the book. 

Personally I think this moral ambiguity is purposeful (cf. the almost complete lack of direct exposition about the defendant's character, perhaps even his total effacement). 

It's only in this space of ambiguity that the 12 Angry (White) Men can project _their own_ moral ambiguity into the otherwise empty space of the jury room. 

Love being compelled to talk about the craft first thing in the morning. Thanks op!

Good job, you have discovered the concept of jury nullification! Now don’t mention it to anyone else, especially if you ever sit on a jury in the US.

I definitely think the bigotry is one aspect of it; the racist comments from the Ed Begley character, and the very obvious (but still awesome!) scene where the other characters and the film, itself, textually reject those comments.

But I agree with the others that the film is meant to be a microcosm of how people in America interact with the criminal justice system in general. All of them have some degree of fury over it and over each other, righteous or not. After all, it’s 12 Angry Men. Not 3 Angry Men and a Handful of Ambivalent Men. Racism certainly plays a part in that, but ultimately, Id say the overall idea is that boy on trial, regardless of any of his characteristics, deserves a fair, impartial jury just like anyone else. And that means one free of racism, but also free of presumptions in many other aspects, which is what the film dives into.

OP’s stance actually highlights one of the most troublesome aspects of in dubio pro reo. If even a fictional story deliberately written to be ambiguous  brings out biased guilt assumptions from people like OP, who writes “well, what’s with all of that final speech huh? Anyway, I _believe_ he did it”, imagine the day to day of trials.

Technically their post is arguing the other side: they could be guilty but they shouldn’t go to jail. 

 IANAL, but OP’s third paragraph is troubling to me from a legal standpoint. None of their justifications have anything to do with the facts of the case, and applying 2024 social justice to 1957 court movie is also not fair. 

The movie provided reasonable doubt and that’s the benchmark for a conviction.

Isn't Jury Nullification exactly what would be (appropriately) used here per OPs beliefs?

As in: he's guilty but we also don't think he should be punished?

Yeah, can’t have a say on US law, I’m a brazilian lawyer. In Brazil, only a select few cases undergo jury trial, but the overwhelming majority are homicides. Our jury system is completely different from US, as jurors can’t talk to one another, their vote are secret and based on ‘intimate reasoning’ (aka they can’t disclose why they voted the way they did). So OP’s thoughts are troubling to me precisely because of my experience: jurors not paying attention to evidence and relying on ‘gut feeling’ based on the personality and other ‘traits’ of the defendant. Sure, it can go both ways, as you said, which is no less problematic if we think about it.

nah. base on what ? 

The whole point  of the movie is even if it so obvious, there can be more than meet the eye. "He 100% did it, no way all is coincident right  ? there are so much evident ? i mean 1 evident ? sure but there are plenty all that lead to him be the murder" 

that make you so sure he must did it. but guess what ? all the evident get debunk, every one of them. The debunk reason also very logical. most of these likely can debunk and it is not even really hard if i really think about it, if he got a  decent layer.

So now base on what you said he did it ?  even though there are literary no single evident left that support that idea. that mean the whole reason he "100% did it" in the first place is gone. you did exactly what the Juror 3 did. You are prejudice base on his background and what not.

I also remember back when i watch it, there are one mystery, now it been years so i don't really remember what exactly it is, the knife or something. but i do remember that thing make me think: hey, if that mean there are someone else there before the kid come back home ?   and none of the juror remember to go to the bottom of it. But then again, this case is to decide this kid guilty or not. looking for another suspect is not the job here.



So yeah, i don't think he did it, but wait, i also don't think possible of he did not do it  gone 100%, never say never you can write even more plot twist then turn it around again. So to me it more of a blank, the case go back to square one with no prime suspect.

Why does that matter? I don't think the artistic process lacking an answer should really impact whether or not a viewer explores the options. For what its worth, I've always felt like the story only really makes sense to want to tell if one operates under the general idea of "innocent until proven guilty" and the film's central theme is that his guilt has not been proven. If ambiguity and the process is the attractive part of the story then I don't think it's such a stretch to feel like the author's assume innocence as well.

I guess? Like I said, IANAL, but if the facts of the case cause reasonable doubt then isn’t it more accurate to vote not guilty on that basis rather than bring up jury nullification?

What happens if the opposite scenario is true? That the evidence eliminates reasonable doubt and that the defendant murdered the victim and there was nothing justifying killing the victim. If everything OP wrote still applies, claiming “he did kill a person, but shouldn’t be punished” outside of specific scenarios would be a lot harder to argue.

Maybe, that's why I asked. I'm not a law expert, but I find the fact that our law institutions try so hard to obscure the existence of jury nullification extremely suspect and a reason unto itself to consider it and spread around its existence.

Maybe it would not have a been appropriate for 12 Angry Men, but your example defies the point of it. If there is no specific scenario making the murder justified to a majority of 12 people, then a nullification wouldnt happen. That seems no different than a guilty or innocent verdict. Just another available option to ensure justice, and not a blind adherence to gamesmanship and rules lawyering prevails.

>The film is meant to highlight our bigotry and by extension, USA's bigotry as a whole.

No, that is not how I see or think about the movie.

You treat the movie as a puzzle with one and only one rational, objective solution; then, you imply it is your task and the task of each viewer to find that solution.

That is not how I experience and think about that movie.

Justice is blind.  To me, that the twelve jurors reach a verdict says little about whether the defendant committed the crime; and says only if he is guilty or not guilty in a courtroom.  Neither of those is a puzzle, certainly not the latter.  Justice is not a puzzle.  How strangely you write about this movie.

>Personally, I do believe he did it. Would I have said "Not Guilty"? I would.

One problem with that is the movie is not titled "13 Angry Men" or "12 Angry Men in a Movie and a Viewer not in It."  You are eavesdropping on jury deliberations and have no say in the verdict.  From your comment you imply every viewer is a member of the jury and that is not what the movie presents.  You have put yourself into a movie where you do not belong.  I too do not belong in that movie.
